paragraphs.title: Introduction
paragraphs.p: Trigonometry, Math123 is designed to give you tools to succeed in various programs in science, such as health professions, geology, and biology.

paragraphs.title: Course Description

blockquote.p: Math123 is a study of oscillatory behavior, circular functions, and their applications. In order to understand these things, it is important to see where they arise. This means analyzing data or situations, choosing among appropriate models, and solving applied problems. Of course, we can't predict every situation you will encounter in your future, so it is also important to develop flexibility and resilience.

paragraphs.p: More information can be found in and .

paragraphs.title: Learning is fun!
paragraphs.p: Learning is about feeding our curiosity, stretching ourselves to be better, finding out, and understanding. Those things are all rewarding, which is another word for fun. When learning isn't fun, there is something badly wrong.
You know what isn't fun? Grades. Getting them, assigning them, working for them none of these things are fun. They are, in many ways, the opposite of fun.

A growing body of evidence shows essentially no correlation between grades and success in future endeavors. Anecdotal evidence and educational research support the idea that grades, in fact, create a dis-incentive for learning and create incentives for several negative behaviors, including engaging in academic dishonesty (cheating). Neuroscience research further shows that dopamine is critical for learning, except in the case of learning with punishment. In other words, you need fun to learn. See, for example,
One thing we will do in this course is remove the pressure of the grade using a version of specifications grading that is sometimes called ungrading. More details are in .

paragraphs.title: Math is fun!
paragraphs.p: Many of you may have an experience of mathematics that does not suggest math is fun. Even if you know and appreciate the usefulness of math, the subject is often presented in a way that sucks all the fun out of it. Imagine sitting down to play a video game and finding that before you can actually start playing the game, you must first spend hours and hours memorizing cheat codes! Now we need to master the up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A, Start sequence and its variations. This will make later games easier. Enter this sequence 35 times on the next screen.

This is nothing like what mathematics really is. Yes, sometimes memorizing techniques can make later things easier, but these techniques have deeper meanings and origins. They are not just a random sequence of buttons to push.

Instead, mathematics is about analyzing situations, carefully describing or quantifying them, and looking for (more or less universal) patterns. That may still sound dry, but my personal goal in this class, in addition to giving you useful techniques, is to help you to see the beauty and joy of mathematics.

paragraphs.title: Additional Content
paragraphs.p: In addition to developing mathematical tools, techniques, and skills, we will seek to further our understanding of the role and importance of mathematics as a not only a tool, but as a field of human endeavor. We will explore how various concepts have developed and evolved, and how various mathematical models are interrelated.

subsection.title: Introduction to Ungrading
subsection.p: As mentioned earlier, substantial evidence shows that grades and grading are inherently antithetical to learning. Ungrading shifts the goal of a course from achievement to learning.

It is also important to note that the content of this course focuses on developing conceptual and procedural fluency with a set of concepts and tools as well as developing a mathematical mindset. Thus, it makes sense to have learning targets that students need to satisfy in order to consider the course successful.

Ultimately, though, this is your course. It is you who are the learner, and so you are in the best position to determine what will be of the most interest, what will be the most engaging, and, beyond the basics, what will be of the most value to you. More than that, you are the best person to determine how much you have learned. Therefore, you will be an active participant in determining the direction of the course and in your evaluation.

To put things bluntly, I will determine, based on a set of learning targets and a body of evidence that you present to me, whether you have done the basic minimum to pass the class. Beyond that, you will determine your own grade, based on your own goals and your own assessment of your learning, as outlined in , .

subsection.title: Portfolio and Reader's Guide
subsection.p: During the first week of class, we will discuss as a class what success in this class might look like, and then you will meet individually with me to develop a set of personalized goals.
These goals will not about grades and grading. Instead, you are invited to consider your learning, and more generally what success in this course will be for you.

Over the course of the semester, you will assemble a comprehensive portfolio that demonstrates that you have met the basic requirements for the course and demonstrates your progress toward your goals. We will meet periodically to discuss your progress, your successes, and any challenges you are facing. My tentative plan is to meet with each student approximately every three weeks at a minimum.

Between meetings, you are expected to submit items to me for focused feedback. Based on this feedback, you will reflect, rework, extend, and revise as necessary to meet basic requirements and show forward progress.

For each individual meeting, you will create a guide, or road map, for the reader (your instructor) in which you discuss your progress. This guide should discuss successes, challenges, and progress, and should direct the reader where to find evidence of these items. For example, you might include something along the lines of Successes Since our last meeting, I have reviewed and improved my understanding of difference quotients and average rate of change. Some good examples of my understanding and interpretation can be found in Driving North/South and Filling a Tank.These titles are completely invented and may not be anything like the titles of activities we actually use.

At each check-in, we will use your reader's guide to navigate the portfolio, and we will discuss your progress. In particular, we will focus on these questions:
What are you particularly proud of or excited about?
What has been challenging?
What do you plan to do next?, and
What do you need from me (the instructor) to facilitate your progress toward your goals?

For your final portfolio conference, which will be during the week of final exams, you will submit your final portfolio (with a final version of your reader's guide), again citing items of interest. Then, based on your learning and progress toward your goals and your submitted evidence, you will tell me what grade you have earned for the course.

subsubsection.title: Catalog of Detailed Examples
subsubsection.p: Over the course of the semester we will be study circular/trigonometric functions, their graph and inverse function, vectors, complex numbers and polar coordinates, trigonometric identities, and triangles.

For each topic, whenever possible, you must include at least one detailed example of the use of that concept in a practical setting. That is, each example must:
Begin with a practical situation where the numbers have units and meaning.
Include a discussion of why the particular concept or tool was used (possibly including why other approaches would not be appropriate).
Show the process of using the concept to understand and solve the problem.
Include multiple representations, such as graphical, numerical, and algebraic representations.
Interpret the solution in context, giving a result with practical implications.

subsubsection.title: Overviews of Activities, Techniques, and Applications
subsubsection.p: Over the course of the semester you will be assigned multiple activities, investigations, and projects dealing with techniques, concepts, and applications from trigonometry.
For each topic we study, not each activity, you are expected to demonstrate understanding of the main mathematical ideas and an ability to apply any associated techniques.
Like everything in the portfolio, these are works in progress, and you are expected to revisit them in light of later activities or readings that may change your understanding of them.

introduction.p: This course is subject to the GVSU policies listed at . The following policies also apply.

Use of Generative AI Large Language Models [LLMs] (such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, etc.) in this class is subject to a few conditions, namely , , and . Transparency and accountability are fairly straight-forward, and are closely related to , , but awareness is both more subtle and arguably more important.

subsubsection.title: Awareness
subsubsection.p: If you plan to use generative AI in this class, be aware of what you are using it for and whether it helps you toward your goals or just wastes your time. I find a useful analogy to be the idea of taking a forklift to the gym.

If your goal in going to the gym is to strengthen your muscles by lifting weights, using a forklift to lift the weights defeats the purpose. Sure, you can get in your reps, you can lift more than you could without the forklift, and you can do more reps and not get tired, but it doesn't work toward your goal of strengthening your muscles. It is a waste of your time. Worse, it gets in other people's way as they try to reach their strength training goals.

On the other hand, maybe you went to the gym because you work there and the boss wants you to move several large, heavy machines from one part of the building to another. If that's the case, using the forklift makes a lot of sense, because it is in fact helping with your goal of moving the machines.
Education is about strengthening your mental muscles. Be aware of how the use of heavy machinery either helps or hinders your progress.

Awareness also includes awareness of the ethical and practical pitfalls involved in using generative AI. You should be aware that
AI is trained on the works of other people
Plausibility, not objective truth, is the training goal of AI. It often makes things up that sound plausible.
AI is resource intensive. For example, according to , a paragraph of AI generated text uses more than 23 times as much electricity and water than a Google search without AI.

subsubsection.title: Transparency
subsubsection.p: When you use generative AI, be transparent: make note of exactly what you asked the AI to do (your prompts), and exactly what part of the AI results you used in your materials. For example, you might include something like the following in your portfolio.

p.q: In this problem, we were asked to model the number of hours of daylight as a function of the date. I knew this would be either sine or cosine, but I still didn't understand how to make the right days line up with the peaks and valleys, so I asked Copilot to explain. My prompt was Explain how to shift a sine function so that the peaks and valleys line up with data.

Copilot started by giving a formula for a sine function as y=A\sin\big(B(x-C)\big)+D and then gave step-by-step alignment guide. The important part for me was how to adjust the phase shift, C. It said to Find where a peak (or valley) occurs in your data, and shift the sine wave so its peak matches that point: C = x\text{-value of desired peak}. I was then able to align the peak amount of sunlight with June 21 by using C=172 days since the beginning of the year.

subsubsection.title: Accountability
subsubsection.p: When you use generative AI, you are accountable. What that means is that you must be able to explain all of your work and understand the power and the limitations of using LLMs.

Using the example of fitting a sine wave, a student submitting this should have noticed that Copilot got it wrong. Setting C=172 places the midline of the sine function at x=172 days. Using C=172 in the formula y=A\cos\big(B(x-C)\big)+D would place the peak at x=172, or you could find the date of the spring equinox and set C to that value in y=A\sin\big(B(x-C)\big)+D.

subsection.title: Time Management
subsection.p: One of my goals for this course is to challenge you to grow intellectually while giving you the tools and environment that will allow you to succeed. If you at any time feel that you are not being challenged to achieve your fullest potential in understanding the concepts we address, or if you have comments about the pace of the class or any other concerns, I encourage you to discuss your concerns with me during my student hours or an appointment with me.

As a university mathematics course, you should expect the course to be challenging. While we will all work to make time spent in class as productive as possible, it is not possible to learn everything using class time alone: much of your learning and understanding will occur as you reflect on what we have done in class, work on problems, and read and discuss course material outside of class.

The most important rule for this course is do not get behind in your work. Using a portfolio removes the inherent penalties in a slow start, but the trade off is that it can be tempting to put things off until later. Always stay up to date with the material in this course. Make succeeding in this course a priority!

introduction.p: Learning cannot take place solely in the classroom, and you should expect to put in considerable work outside of class. Different students learn in different ways and require different types of support. I am committed to providing you with the support that you require, whether that means being a critical questioner of your processes and results, providing guidance and mentoring, or something else entirely.
This section has some advice and perspectives that I hope will help you make the most of your time and effort in this class.

subsubsection.title: Attend Student Hours
subsubsection.p: First, never hesitate to come to me during student hours or to make an appointment to see me. My primary job is to facilitate your understanding and learning, so when you come to me you are allowing me to do my job well.

subsubsection.title: Form a Study Group
subsubsection.p: You may also find that working with a group of classmates is beneficial. I encourage you to form groups to work together outside of class. Working with a group also allows you to see things from different perspectives.

If you or your study group have questions, please come to me and we will work through them together. If my student hours are at times that you cannot make due to other commitments, make an appointment to see me at another time.

subsubsection.title: Make Attendance a Priority
subsubsection.p: As discussed in , attendance in class is an important part of this course. You are expected to be present and on time each day we meet. You are responsible for announcements made in class concerning material covered, assignments, changes in the syllabus or due dates, or anything else pertinent to the course. Furthermore, many of the activities from class and reflections on class will become part of your portfolio.

Nevertheless, your health and safety and that of your classmates is important. Therefore if you are ill, stay at home. In the event of a University recognized absence, arrangements can be made for you to mitigate the effects of missing class.

subsubsection.title: Come to Class Prepared
subsubsection.p: It is imperative that you work on a consistent basis. This applies to both the day-to-day work to prepare for class as well as the more long-term work such as the portfolio.

You should keep a well-organized record of your study notes, completed problems, and problems in progress for future reference. Note that these are acceptable as part of your portfolio if you believe they help make your case!

You must understand that a great deal of your learning in this course must occur on your own. It is your responsibility to complete assigned reading, read assignments carefully, complete the problems, be prepared for class, and to seek support as needed.

subsubsection.title: Participate in Class
subsubsection.p: For many people, their experience has taught them that asking questions or questioning results is frowned on as either disrespectful or inattentive. In this class, I want to cultivate an atmosphere where questioning processes, results, and reasoning is seen as showing respect that the other person's ideas are worth thinking about. This type of respectful questioning (including questioning your own processes, thoughts, and results) is crucial to becoming an effective and flexible thinker.

Asking and answering questions are not the only ways, or even the best ways, to participate in class. While we may think of class participation in terms of speaking up in class, participation can take many forms, such as active listening in groups, writing up or journaling individual or group assignments, drawing graphs or creating visual representations, sharing strategies, questioning results, and many others. In every class meeting, there will be ample opportunity for you to actively participate.

subsubsection.title: Make Full Use of Additional Learning Resources
subsubsection.p: The idea of asking for help can sometimes take on a negative connotation. I prefer to think of it as one way to make use of all of your available resources. If you need to travel from the Allendale campus to the Grand Rapids, you probably don't think that taking the Laker Line instead driving a car is a bad thing, it's simply another effective way to travel. And there are also lots of reasons why some students might not have access to a car, including having a flat tire or not having a license. In a similar way, there are lots of reasons to seek out additional learning resources.

In addition to student hours and individual meetings with me, GVSU provides a variety of tutoring resources, including the Math Center (located in Mackinac Hall). More information about other tutoring services can be found on the GVSU Tutoring website.
Using these resources is smart, and can be beneficial to every student.

subsubsection.title: Integrity of Scholarship and Grades
subsubsection.p: Truth and honesty: The principles of truth and honesty are recognized as fundamental to a community of teachers and scholars. The university expects that both faculty members and students will honor these principles and in so doing protect the validity of university grades. This means that all academic work will be done by the student to whom it is assigned without unauthorized aid of any kind. Instructors, for their part, will exercise care in the planning and supervision of academic work, so that honest effort will be positively encouraged. Compliance shall include compliance with the following specific rules:

li.p: No student shall knowingly, without authorization, procure, provide, or accept any materials which contain questions or answers to any examination or assignment.
No student shall, without authorization, complete, in part or in total, any examination or assignment for another person.
No student shall, without authorization, allow any examination or assignment to be completed, in part or in total, by another person.
No student shall knowingly plagiarize or copy the work of another person and submit it as his or her own.

No student shall submit work that has been previously graded or is being submitted concurrently to more than one course without authorization from the instructor(s) of the class(es) to which the student wishes to submit it.

subsubsection.title: Plagiarism
subsubsection.p: Any ideas or material taken from another source for either written or oral presentation must be fully acknowledged. Offering the work of someone else as one's own is plagiarism. The language or ideas taken from another may range from isolated formulas, sentences, or paragraphs to entire articles copied from books, periodicals, speeches, or the writing of other students. The offering of materials assembled or collected by others in the form of projects or collections without acknowledgment also is considered plagiarism. Any student who fails to give credit in written or oral work for the ideas or materials that have been taken from another is guilty of plagiarism.
Such activity may result in failure of a specific assignment, an entire course, or, if flagrant, dismissal from Grand Valley. For further information see Student Rights and Responsibilities.

subsubsection.p:
In the event that we meet virtually via Zoom, class meetings will be recorded and will be available to students enrolled in this course as a study aid.
